source.title: Massively Multilingual Instruction-Following Information Extraction
source.authors: Thang Le; Huy Huu Nguyen; A. Lưu; T. Nguyen

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether model scaling improves downstream multilingual IE performance, using LF1 task scores rather than pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites neural scaling laws and tests parameter scaling on downstream IE performance. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or loss extrapolation. Results of cited work are not treated as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: It compares released models of different sizes within the same family on a new downstream setting, multilingual IE (LF1 on M-LIGHT), under few-shot ICL and SFT. This bears on V6. It fits no power law and measures no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors state that 'neural scaling laws still hold for multilingual IE' under few-shot ICL, with monotonic within-family gains. For SFT they say scaling generally holds but is less significant and non-monotonic (Qwen2.5). Their overall conclusion is that multilingual IE remains very challenging for current LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream multilingual IE LF1 performance across released model sizes rather than held-out pretraining loss across controlled training runs. It does not fit power laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling pattern differs between few-shot ICL and SFT; SFT scaling is less pronounced and non-monotonic.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of ACL 2025)
record.problems: The scaling results are described qualitatively in the prose, without uncertainty estimates or numeric per-size scaling results there. The experiments measure downstream LF1, not pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 5 and 6 report task-level SFT scores for multiple models, but those cross-family results do not isolate parameter scaling; the direct scaling comparisons are summarized in Appendix E.2 and Figures 21–22.

untested.parts: Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; any quantitative fit or prediction of downstream scores from smaller models ('predictably' in the strict sense); controlled training runs rather than released checkpoints.
Not tested: no pretraining loss measured.
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: fine-tuning results are task scores, not a power-law form.

missing.what: Within-family SFT comparison Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct vs 8B-Instruct: avg LF1 64.15 vs 64.98; NER 72.98 vs 73.89, SF 74.40 vs 81.16, EE 49.53 vs 51.54. The larger model is slightly worse; 70B used QLoRA. rows_left_out wrongly calls the table only cross-family.
Per-size numeric SFT scores for Qwen2.5 3B/7B/14B/32B on M-LIGHT mixed (avg 61.92/63.65/66.88/67.21) and M-HEAVY mixed (avg 53.35/55.28/57.52/59.14), with per-task non-monotonicity
Under 3B, most models fail to give reasonable outputs (except Qwen2.5-3B); performance is near zero below a size threshold

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new downstream setting that evaluates released checkpoints, not a controlled scaling study. 'Scaling laws' is used loosely; no power-law fit is made, so 'predictable' improvement is supported only in the sense of monotonic gains. The scaling analysis is a minor part of a benchmark paper. Sizes are confounded with release differences across family members.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how either changes with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests parameter scaling on multilingual IE task performance, but not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and bending of loss curves.

rows.subject: same model families (scaling comparisons; aggregate statement)
rows.size_stated: 21 LLMs ranging from 0.5B to 72B; sizes of the compared family members are not stated in the prose
rows.operation_detail: Compared few-shot multilingual IE performance across parameter sizes within model families.

conditions.value: default few-shot prompts; 3 English demonstrations per task

rows.measure: Multilingual IE task performance as parameter count increases
rows.value: The authors report a monotonic trend, with significantly better results at larger parameter counts in each task within the same model family.
rows.note: The prose reports a family-level aggregate trend, not separate numeric outcomes for each model or task. The authors also give Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct versus Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as an example of a large performance increase.
rows.check: Linkage and state are fine. The size ranges are not stated per family; Figure 4 is not quantified in the prose. The text also says most models under 3B produce no reasonable output, which suggests a threshold rather than a smooth trend. The 70B vs 8B example is described only as 'several times better'.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 series
rows.size_stated: 3B, 7B, 14B, and 32B models are named in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Compared SFT multilingual IE performance across parameter sizes in the Qwen2.5 series.
rows.measure: Multilingual IE task performance as parameter count increases
rows.value: The authors report an increasing but non-monotonic trend, with a smaller difference than in few-shot ICL.
rows.note: The result is described across the Qwen2.5 series; per-size and per-task values are not given in the prose.
rows.check: Figure 21 is not numeric, but Table 5 gives within-family values that the row should record. Qwen2.5 3B/7B/14B/32B average LF1 is 61.92/63.65/66.88/67.21, monotonic on average. Per task it is non-monotonic: EE 49.46/48.59/53.60/50.73, and NER, RE and ED are also close or flat. The baseline should be the 3B model.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 series
rows.size_stated: 3B, 7B, 14B, and 32B models are named in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Compared SFT multilingual IE performance across parameter sizes in the Qwen2.5 series.
rows.measure: Multilingual IE task performance as parameter count increases
rows.value: The authors characterize SFT scaling as generally holding but less significant than ICL, and describe the parameter trend as increasing but non-monotonic.
rows.note: The result is described across the Qwen2.5 series; per-size and per-task values are not given in the prose.
rows.check: Zero-shot values in Figure 22 are not given numerically. The appendix statement covers both settings jointly, so the value text is accurate. Table 6 (M-HEAVY mixed) also gives Qwen averages 53.35/55.28/57.52/59.14, monotonic on average but not per task (e.g., ED 50.99/53.76/49.95/52.66). This is not recorded.

relationships.condition: Few-shot ICL, default prompts, within model families (e.g., Qwen2.5 series, Llama-3.1 8B→70B) on M-LIGHT
relationships.reason: Authors report LF1 rising monotonically with parameter count in each task within families (r1). The trend is qualitative and has no fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported increasing LF1 at every tested parameter size for each task within model families.

relationships.condition: SFT (LoRA) on Qwen2.5 3B–32B, mixed and zero-shot settings
relationships.reason: Gains are smaller than in ICL and non-monotonic per task. Table 5 averages go 61.92→67.21, but EE peaks at 14B (r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Average scores rose from 61.92 to 67.21, but event extraction peaked at 14B and gains were smaller than with in-context learning.

relationships.condition: SFT of Llama-3.1 8B vs 70B (70B trained with 4-bit QLoRA), M-LIGHT mixed
relationships.reason: Based on Table 5 text, not a row: 70B averages 64.15 vs 64.98 for 8B, worse on NER, SF and EE. The comparison is confounded by QLoRA, which the authors suspect is unstable.
relationships.display_finding: The 70B model averaged 64.15 versus 8B's 64.98 and performed worse on NER, SF, and EE, although potentially unstable QLoRA confounded the comparison.
